name: Abel Tasman National Park
tagline: A golden-sand, sea-kissed national park where a coastal track, sheltered bays and a water-taxi network make wilderness feel completely unhurried.
highlight: Stepping off a water taxi onto an empty golden-sand beach reachable no other way, with native bush rising straight behind it.
shortDescription: New Zealand's smallest national park, its golden beaches, sheltered bays and coastal track making it the country's easiest wilderness to enjoy.
metaDescription: An Abel Tasman National Park travel guide: the Coast Track, Split Apple Rock, kayaking, when to go and how to plan a day trip or multi-day walk.
knownFor: Golden beaches, the Coast Track, sea kayaking, water taxis
goodFor: Coastal walking, kayaking, beaches without the crowds

image.file: File:Anchorage Bay, Abel Tasman National Park (16351895238).jpg
image.alt: The golden sand of Anchorage Bay in Abel Tasman National Park

intro: Abel Tasman is New Zealand's smallest national park, but its combination of golden-sand beaches, clear sheltered water and native coastal bush has made it one of the country's most popular — more accessible than the South Island's bigger, more remote wilderness areas.

Its defining feature is the Abel Tasman Coast Track, one of New Zealand's Great Walks, though the park is just as rewarding for a single day: a water taxi can drop you at a beach in the morning and pick you up further along the coast in the afternoon, no multi-day hike required.
Kaiteriteri and Marahau, the two small gateway towns, give the park a relaxed, beach-holiday feel that's distinct from the more dramatic mountain scenery found elsewhere on the South Island.

whyVisit.intro: Abel Tasman's case rests on making South Island wilderness easy — golden beaches and coastal bush without a demanding multi-day commitment.

points.title: It's the most accessible of New Zealand's Great Walks
points.text: Water taxis let you sample any stretch of the Coast Track in a single day, no overnight gear required.

points.title: The beaches are golden-sand and unusually warm for the South Island
points.text: Sheltered bays like Anchorage and Bark Bay stay warm enough to swim through much of the year.

points.title: Split Apple Rock is one of the South Island's most photographed natural curiosities
points.text: A giant granite boulder split cleanly in two, sitting just offshore.

points.title: The kayaking is among the best in the country
points.text: Calm, sheltered water and a dramatic coastline make it an easy, rewarding paddle for any skill level.

points.title: It's a short, easy add-on to a Nelson or Marlborough trip
points.text: Close enough to Nelson Airport to combine easily with the rest of the northern South Island.

attractionsIntro: Abel Tasman's essential sights span its golden bays, its coastal track, and a scattering of natural curiosities along the shore.

attractions.name: Anchorage Bay

image.file: File:Anchorage Bay, Abel Tasman National Park (16351895238).jpg
image.alt: The golden sand beach at Anchorage Bay

attractions.text: A classic Abel Tasman beach, its wide golden sand and calm water a popular water-taxi drop-off and the first night's stop on the Coast Track.
attractions.tip: Arrive on an early water taxi for the quietest hours before day-trip crowds build.

attractions.name: Split Apple Rock

image.alt: Split Apple Rock, a granite boulder split cleanly in two off the Abel Tasman coast

attractions.text: A striking granite boulder sitting just offshore, split cleanly down the middle by centuries of frost and erosion.
attractions.tip: It's visible from a short beach walk near Kaiteriteri, no boat required.

attractions.name: The Abel Tasman Coast Track

image.file: File:View from Abel Tasman Coastal Track down rocky coast near Ratakura Point.jpg
image.alt: A view along the Abel Tasman Coast Track

attractions.text: A gentle Great Walk by New Zealand standards, 60km of well-formed coastal trail linking golden beaches and native bush.
attractions.tip: Walking just one section between water-taxi stops gives a full taste without committing to all three to five days.

attractions.name: Cleopatra's Pool

image.file: File:Cleopatras Pool, Abel Tasman National Park.jpg
image.alt: Cleopatra's Pool, a natural rock pool and slide in Abel Tasman National Park

attractions.text: A fun natural rock pool fed by a stream, with a smooth rock chute that doubles as a natural water slide.
attractions.tip: A short detour off the main track near Torrent Bay — worth the extra 20 minutes.

attractions.name: Tonga Island Marine Reserve

image.alt: Tonga Island, home to a New Zealand fur seal colony

attractions.text: A protected marine reserve home to a resident New Zealand fur seal colony, easily seen by kayak or water taxi.
attractions.tip: Seals are most active and visible on calm, sunny mornings.

attractions.name: Kaiteriteri Beach

image.alt: The golden sand of Kaiteriteri Beach, gateway to Abel Tasman

attractions.text: The park's genuine gateway beach, a golden crescent with its own resort-town holiday atmosphere and the main water-taxi departure point.
attractions.tip: It's worth a swim here even before or after your time in the park itself.

attractions.name: Bark Bay

image.alt: A kayak on the beach at Bark Bay in Abel Tasman National Park

attractions.text: A quieter beach further up the coast, its tidal lagoon and swing bridge a favourite lunch stop for kayakers and walkers alike.
attractions.tip: Time your visit around the tide — the lagoon crossing is easier near low water.

thingsToDoIntro: Abel Tasman rewards getting onto the water and the track alike, with water taxis making both easy to combine.

thingsToDo.title: Walk a section of the Coast Track

image.file: File:View from Abel Tasman Coastal Track down rocky coast near Ratakura Point.jpg
image.alt: Walking the Abel Tasman Coast Track

thingsToDo.text: An easy, well-formed trail — even a single 2-3 hour stretch between water-taxi stops covers the park's best coastal scenery.
thingsToDo.tip: The Anchorage to Torrent Bay stretch is one of the most scenic and manageable short sections.

thingsToDo.title: Kayak the coastline

image.file: File:Sea Kayaking Abel Tasman National Park.jpg
image.alt: Sea kayaking along the Abel Tasman coastline

thingsToDo.text: Guided and freedom kayak trips let you paddle right up to Split Apple Rock and Tonga Island's seal colony.
thingsToDo.tip: A half-day guided trip needs no prior kayaking experience.

thingsToDo.title: Swim and slide at Cleopatra's Pool

image.file: File:Cleopatras Pool, Abel Tasman National Park.jpg
image.alt: Swimming at Cleopatra's Pool

thingsToDo.text: A refreshing detour off the main track, cool freshwater and a natural rock slide that's popular with kids and adults alike.
thingsToDo.tip: Water levels vary with recent rainfall — the slide works best after some rain upstream.

thingsToDo.title: Take a water taxi to a remote beach

image.alt: A water taxi in Abel Tasman National Park

thingsToDo.text: The park's defining convenience — get dropped at one beach and walk or get picked up from another, no return leg required.
thingsToDo.tip: Book both legs of a drop-off and pick-up together — timing matters more than it seems.

thingsToDo.title: Spot fur seals at Tonga Island

image.alt: Tonga Island Marine Reserve, home to a fur seal colony

thingsToDo.text: A reliable wildlife stop by kayak or boat cruise, with seals regularly hauled out on the rocks.
thingsToDo.tip: Keep a respectful distance — this is a protected marine reserve.

thingsToDo.title: Relax at Kaiteriteri Beach

image.alt: Relaxing on Kaiteriteri Beach

thingsToDo.text: An easy, low-key way to bookend a day in the park, with a proper swimming beach and cafés right at the water taxi terminal.
thingsToDo.tip: Arrive early in summer — the car park fills up fast on warm days.

foodIntro: Abel Tasman's food options are simple and beach-town casual, centred on Kaiteriteri and Marahau rather than the park itself.

foods.name: Green-lipped mussels

image.alt: A plate of New Zealand green-lipped mussels

foods.text: The wider Nelson-Marlborough region is mussel-farming country, and they appear steamed and simply prepared on local menus.

foods.name: Whitebait fritters

image.file: File:Whitebait fritter sandwich Nosh Cafe Waimate.jpg
image.alt: A whitebait fritter, a South Island seasonal delicacy

foods.text: A genuine seasonal treat when local rivers are running, tiny native fish bound in a light egg batter.
foods.whereToTry: Cafés in Motueka during the spring whitebait season.

foods.name: Fish and chips

image.alt: A classic New Zealand fish and chips takeaway

foods.text: A reliable, casual choice after a day on the track or the water, sold at both gateway towns.

foods.name: Hokey pokey ice cream

image.alt: Hokey pokey ice cream, a New Zealand favourite

foods.text: A perfect match for a hot beach afternoon, vanilla ice cream studded with honeycomb toffee.

foods.name: Manuka honey

image.alt: Jars of New Zealand manuka honey

foods.text: The Tasman region's abundant native bush makes it good manuka country, sold direct from small producers nearby.

foods.name: Flat white

image.file: File:Flat white coffee Highgate Cricket Club, Crouch End, London 01.jpg
image.alt: A flat white coffee, a New Zealand café staple

foods.text: Essential before an early water taxi, and both gateway towns keep a steady café standard.

accommodation.intro: Kaiteriteri and Marahau are the two main gateway bases, both right at the water-taxi departure points.

areas.name: Kaiteriteri
areas.bestFor: A beach-resort atmosphere with the widest range of accommodation
areas.text: The busier, more developed of the two gateway towns, with its own popular swimming beach.

areas.name: Marahau
areas.bestFor: The closest access to the start of the Coast Track
areas.text: A quieter, smaller settlement right at the park boundary.

areas.name: Motueka
areas.bestFor: A cheaper, more local base a short drive away
areas.text: A practical small town with a wider choice of budget accommodation and services.

gettingThere.intro: Abel Tasman is reached via Nelson, with Kaiteriteri and Marahau both under an hour's drive from the airport.

options.text: About 50-60 minutes' drive from Nelson Airport to Kaiteriteri or Marahau.
Scheduled shuttles connect Nelson to both gateway towns.
options.detail: An easy option for visitors without a rental car.

options.mode: Rental car or bus from Picton
options.text: About 2 hours' drive, useful if arriving via the Interislander ferry.
options.detail: A workable link for visitors road-tripping up from the North Island.

gettingAround.intro: Within the park itself, boats do most of the work, since there's no road access beyond the gateway towns.

options.text: The standard way to reach any beach or track section without walking the full length.
options.detail: Frequent scheduled services run from both Kaiteriteri and Marahau.

options.text: The Coast Track itself is the only way to move between bays on land.
options.detail: Well-formed and gentle by Great Walk standards, suitable for most fitness levels.

options.text: A flexible, self-paced way to explore the coastline and reach Tonga Island.
options.detail: Both guided trips and independent rentals are widely available.

bestTime.headline: Spring through autumn for the warmest, driest walking and swimming conditions
bestTime.summary: Abel Tasman's sheltered position makes it one of the sunniest, driest parts of the South Island.

seasons.text: Warm and reliable for swimming, though the busiest season on the track and beaches.
Settled weather with noticeably thinner crowds than summer.
Cooler and quieter, though still mild enough for walking without snow.
Increasingly warm, a good shoulder season before summer's crowds arrive.

bestTime.avoid: Nothing strongly, though book water taxis and Great Walk huts well ahead for the December–February peak.

itinerary.title: Two days in Abel Tasman
itinerary.intro: Built around a full day exploring the coast by boat and track, with time on Kaiteriteri's beach either side.

days.title: Water taxi and Coast Track
days.morning: Water taxi to Anchorage Bay or Bark Bay.
days.afternoon: Walk a scenic section of the Coast Track back toward Marahau, with a stop at Cleopatra's Pool.

days.title: Kayaking and the coast
days.summary: A slower day on the water.
days.morning: A guided kayak trip past Split Apple Rock to Tonga Island.
days.afternoon: Swim and relax at Kaiteriteri Beach.

tipsIntro: Practical notes on booking, tides and timing that make a real difference to an Abel Tasman trip.
tips: Book water taxis ahead in summer — the popular morning departures sell out.
Check tide times before planning a walk near Torrent Bay's lagoon crossing.
Bring plenty of sun protection — the sheltered coast is sunnier than much of the South Island.
Pack light, waterproof day gear even in summer — coastal weather can change quickly.
Book Great Walk huts and campsites well ahead if walking the full track in peak season.
Combine a water-taxi drop-off with a walk back rather than a return boat trip for better value.

faq.q: Do you need to walk the full Coast Track to enjoy Abel Tasman?
faq.a: No, not — water taxis let you sample any single section in a day, and this is how most visitors experience the park.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Abel Tasman?
faq.a: Two days covers a water taxi and walk combination plus kayaking comfortably. The full Coast Track takes three to five days.

faq.q: Is Abel Tasman good for kids?
faq.a: Yes — the short walking sections, calm swimming beaches and Cleopatra's Pool's rock slide all suit families well.

faq.q: Can you see Split Apple Rock without a boat?
faq.a: Yes — it's visible from a short beach walk near Kaiteriteri, though kayaking gets you closer.

faq.q: Is Kaiteriteri or Marahau the better base?
faq.a: Kaiteriteri has more of a resort-town feel and swimming beach; Marahau sits right at the Coast Track's start for an earlier departure.

faq.q: Do you need a car in Abel Tasman?
faq.a: Not within the park itself — water taxis and the track handle all movement — though a car helps reach Nelson and Motueka.
